items.item: Server is the only writer of Gold; client never sends amounts or prices
Validates remote arguments (types, NaN/inf, bounds) and rate-limits shop requests
Avoids yields between balance check and deduction (atomic spend)
Persistence handled safely (UpdateAsync or session-locked profile; load-before-play; BindToClose)
Does not treat leaderstats as source of truth
Kill rewards awarded by server-side kill attribution, not a client 'I killed X' remote

incorrect_or_stale: BindToClose spawns the saves and then waits a fixed 3 seconds instead of waiting for them to finish, while retry backoff can run past 15 seconds, so shutdown saves can be lost
A held session lock cancels the load right away and kicks the player, with no wait for the lock to clear, so a normal quick rejoin or server hop gets kicked
If the player leaves while the load is still yielding, sessions[player] is set afterwards and the lock is never released (it only expires when stale)
There is no itemId length cap (a minor gap)
slop: 'Add an anomaly check' (flag players earning more than X gold per minute) is generic advice

incorrect_or_stale: Decision 7 says removing the session first means a late reward 'can't be lost mid-save', but it actually means late rewards are rejected and dropped
It cites 'references/currency.md' and 'E2' evidence levels that do not exist for the user
slop: An internal 'Apex route' preamble and '.apex/ memory' meta-commentary that mean nothing to the user
'Not covered' has generic advice like a faucet/sink table and anti-farm rules
overengineering: A token-bucket rate limiter, schema versioning, sanitize and a changed BindableEvent add bulk to an answer that was asked to be concise
Remotes are created at runtime and there are two RemoteEvents (BuyRequest and BuyResult) where one RemoteFunction would do

raw.reason: Both answers meet the core security rubric, but B's persistence is clearly sturdier: it waits for a held lock to clear on rejoin, its BindToClose waits for saves to finish, it sanitizes loaded data and it handles the player leaving mid-load, which outweighs B's meta-noise and extra length compared with A's concise but flawed shutdown and lock handling.
